cl_amph_vs_mph.q: Adderall or Ritalin: which works better, and which has more side effects?
cl_amph_vs_mph.short: Both work. In a review of 133 short trials, amphetamine (as in Adderall) eased symptoms a bit more than methylphenidate (Ritalin). Neither clearly made more people quit over side effects.
cl_amph_vs_mph.but: Few trials tested the two head to head, and none in adults. Most compared one drug with a dummy pill, for a few weeks.
how: A review pooled 133 trials in about 14,300 children and teens and 10,300 adults. On doctors' ratings after about 12 weeks, amphetamine eased symptoms a little more than methylphenidate. The review rated this low certainty.

Quitting because of side effects wasn't clearly different between the two, but a gap wasn't ruled out. Against a dummy pill, more quit on amphetamine at every age, and on methylphenidate in adults. Both lowered weight.

Over about 7 weeks, blood pressure rose by about 1 to 3 points and heart rate by about 2 to 5 beats a minute on average, compared with a dummy pill. The two drugs didn't clearly differ, in 102 trials.

One blinded trial gave 125 children both, two weeks each, with no dummy pill. Parents counted as many complaints on each, but rated sleep and mood ones a bit worse on dexamphetamine, a kind of amphetamine. Many, like irritability (82 in 100), were there before any medicine.
cl_amph_vs_mph.rate: Two big reviews of trials, but few trials tested the two drugs against each other, and none in adults. Trials lasted weeks, and most were paid for by drug makers.

cl_amph_vs_mph_psychosis.q: Is psychosis more likely on Adderall than Ritalin?
cl_amph_vs_mph_psychosis.short: A bit, in one big US study. But it's rare either way. Each year, about 3 in 1,000 people on amphetamine (as in Adderall) had it, against 2 on methylphenidate.
cl_amph_vs_mph_psychosis.but: It's one study of insurance records, not a trial. Things the records missed, like drug use or early signs of illness, could explain part of it.
how: It used records of about 222,000 young people, aged 13 to 25, with ADHD and US insurance. They had started either medicine and were matched on what the records showed.
Over about 4 to 5 months, 343 had a new psychotic episode treated with antipsychotic medicine, about 1 in 650. Per 1,000 people a year, that's 1.8 on methylphenidate and 2.8 on amphetamine.
That's about 1.65 times the rate, or 1 extra case per 1,000 people a year. The paper's own summary, about twice the risk, leaves out that amphetamine starters were followed longer.

Counting psychosis more strictly gave similar results. Emergency or hospital care for alcohol or cannabis wasn't more common after amphetamine. Records can't show the dose, missed drug use, or if pills were taken.
cl_amph_vs_mph_psychosis.rate: One large records study, which matched people on many things and checked other explanations. But it isn't a trial, so differences the records missed, like drug use, could explain part of it.

amphetamine.statement: Studies show people quit Adderall over side effects far more often than Ritalin.
amphetamine.why: In a review of 133 short trials, quitting over side effects wasn't clearly different between amphetamine and methylphenidate, though a gap wasn't ruled out.

amphetamine.statement: Starting Adderall instead of Ritalin doubles the risk of psychosis.
amphetamine.why: In one big records study it was about 1.65 times the rate, about 1 extra case per 1,000 people a year. 'Twice' came from leaving out that amphetamine starters were followed longer.

methylphenidate.statement: In a trial, many 'side effects' blamed on ADHD pills were there before the kids took any.
methylphenidate.why: In one blinded trial of 125 children, parents called 82 in 100 irritable before any medicine was given.

methylphenidate.statement: Psychosis is rare in people who start prescribed ADHD pills.
methylphenidate.why: In 222,000 young people with ADHD, about 2 to 3 in 1,000 a year had a new psychotic episode treated with medicine. That's one records study.
